vignette:
He is a 62-year-old Latin American man who speaks about his life with the careful, measured tone of someone who has spent years trying to keep painful material organized and contained. He is single, and much of his adult identity has been built around work, competence, and the calm authority of his profession as a psychiatrist. Long before he ever enters therapy himself, he has spent decades listening to other people’s suffering, helping them name fear, shame, and grief. He is skilled at recognizing distress in others, but his own trauma feels to him like something that has lived under the surface for so long that it has become part of the architecture of his days.

He describes the beginning of the trauma as a political rupture in his home country, when his earlier life is abruptly overtaken by fear, surveillance, and the certainty that being known can become dangerous. At first he tries to continue working, reasoning that his role as a physician is to remain useful and visible, but the danger tightens around him. He is eventually taken and held by men who treat his body as a site for interrogation rather than a person. The torture is not only physical. He recalls humiliation, deprivation, the distortion of time, and the deliberate use of uncertainty to make him feel that his mind can no longer be trusted. He remembers the sense that each day is designed to erase his dignity in small increments. Even now, he can describe the texture of particular sounds, the smell of the room, the shock of not knowing whether a voice outside the door means rescue or more pain.

Afterward, survival does not feel like relief so much as a strange continuation of danger in a different form. He is eventually able to leave the country, but he arrives in the United States carrying a body that reacts as though the captivity has never ended. For years he works intensely, often to the point of exhaustion, as if productivity can serve as proof that the torture did not defeat him. He becomes a respected psychiatrist, known for his composure and intellectual rigor. Colleagues experience him as thoughtful and contained. What they do not see is how carefully he manages everyday life around reminders he cannot predict. He avoids certain sounds, certain smells, and certain kinds of confinement. Elevators, locked doors, and unexpected footsteps in hallways can provoke a surge of panic that he covers with a neutral expression and a practiced excuse to leave.

In sessions, he speaks of how he still wakes in the night with his heart pounding, often before he can identify a dream. He rarely sleeps through the early hours and becomes increasingly alert as morning approaches, scanning his surroundings in a way that feels automatic rather than chosen. He notices that his body stiffens when someone stands too close behind him, and he is embarrassed by how quickly he can be pulled back into sensations he knows are from the past. At work, he remains highly functional, but he is more irritable than he used to be and more easily exhausted by ordinary demands. He says he has become someone who spends a great deal of energy pretending that he is not always braced for impact.

He also carries a deep, private grief about the person he believes he might have been if the torture had never happened. He wonders whether the years of vigilance have narrowed his life in ways that cannot be measured on the outside. Though he is proud of what he has built, he is lonely in a particular way, reluctant to enter close relationships because intimacy makes him feel exposed. He trusts the language of psychiatry, yet finds it difficult to ask for care himself. He is more comfortable speaking about dissociation, fear, and survival in the abstract than about his own recurrent images of being restrained, his sudden shame when he feels powerless, or the way certain anniversaries and news reports can leave him distant and preoccupied for days.

Still, he keeps returning to therapy. Over time, he begins to notice that what he has long treated as private weakness is the residue of an organized assault on his mind and body. He remains guarded, but there are moments when he speaks less like a clinician and more like the man who endured what he survived, and in those moments the years of silence feel briefly less absolute.
